solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Male warmonger carrying a fighting-axe

indicators.note: whatever carries something holds it, so the male and the warmonger hold the A between them

parts.note: a tom is a male cat
a hawk is a politician keen on war

explanation.surface: A belligerent man goes about armed with a battle-axe.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one man carrying a weapon, but Male and warmonger are separate pieces that hold the A between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A tomahawk is the light axe of North American peoples, used in fighting.

clue.text: Intruder very dated in French resistance

parts.note: passé is French for past it, dated
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: Someone recalls the long-ago days of the French Resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French resistance' wants to be one phrase, the wartime underground, but French belongs with very and dated, and resistance stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A trespasser is someone who intrudes on land without right.

clue.text: Bad name for a soft earthy substance

definitions.meaning: from the idiom saying someone's name is in disgrace

explanation.surface: Some soft, earthy material has been given an unflattering label.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'your name is mud' means you are in disgrace, so mud itself stands for a bad name.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain description of wet soil for one sense; the other is the idiom 'his name is mud', said of someone in disgrace.

clue.text: Musical security device protecting the locks?

parts.note: a PIN is the security number for a bank card

explanation.surface: A tuneful gadget keeps the locks on a door safe.
explanation.walkthrough: Locks look like door locks guarded by a security device, but they are locks of hair, which a hairpin holds in place.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairpin keeps locks of hair in place, so it protects the locks; the question mark flags the pun.

clue.text: Player on pitch, one hanging on to gate

parts.note: a wicket is a small gate
a keeper is one who holds on to something

explanation.surface: A footballer leans on the gate at the edge of the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: The wicketkeeper is the cricket fielder who crouches behind the batsman's stumps; the pieces come in reverse clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: The wicketkeeper is one of the cricket team out on the pitch.

clue.text: Parisian gangster quickly seizing hostage at the outset

indicators.note: seizing means the word for quickly grabs and holds the next letter inside it
at the outset picks just the opening letter of hostage

explanation.surface: A French criminal swiftly grabs a hostage right at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: APACE takes in H, the first letter of 'hostage'.
explanation.definitionFit: An apache was a violent street ruffian in early twentieth-century Paris, so a Parisian gangster.

clue.text: Sound out head of maths about ultimately equivocal sum?

indicators.note: about means the word for sound out goes around the last letter

parts.note: to probe is to sound out

indicators.note: ultimately picks the last letter of equivocal
head of takes the first letter of maths

explanation.surface: A maths teacher sounds out an ambiguous calculation.
explanation.walkthrough: L goes inside PROBE, and M follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A sum set in a maths lesson is a problem to solve; the question mark marks this as an example.

clue.text: Observation about trick over small storage area

indicators.note: something turned over faces the other way

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on a scam involving a little storeroom.
explanation.walkthrough: Small wants to be S, but it belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A compartment is a small separate space for storing things.

clue.text: Predatory type seen in Inverness

indicators.note: the answer can be seen inside the next word

parts.note: letters three to six of the city's name

explanation.surface: A predator has been spotted in the Scottish Highland city.
explanation.walkthrough: The erne, the white-tailed sea eagle, is a crossword regular; it was reintroduced to Scotland, so the surface is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: An erne is a sea eagle, a bird of prey.

clue.text: Scot's weird longing to follow presbyter, not English

indicators.note: to follow is to come after

parts.note: an elder is a presbyter; drop E for English

explanation.surface: A Scotsman has a strange urge to trail after a church elder.
explanation.walkthrough: A presbyter is a church elder; which E goes does not matter, since ELDER without either gives ELDR.
explanation.definitionFit: Eldritch is a Scottish word for weird or eerie.

clue.text: Archer's old wife meeting maiden in bar

indicators.note: the old, wife and maiden letters sit in the word for bar
meeting puts the maiden letter right alongside the wife letter

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for maiden, an over with no runs

explanation.surface: An archer's former wife meets a young woman in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' suggests a pub, but here it is the verb ban.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowman shoots with a bow, so he is an archer.

clue.text: Clinically carving up Italy, visit in any case

indicators.note: cutting Italy up rearranges its letters
ANY is the case that holds the rest

parts.note: to call on is to visit

explanation.surface: An invading power coldly divides up Italy, dropping in anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In any case' reads as a throwaway 'anyway', which is why it slips past as filler; here the word any is a literal case holding everything else.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something clinically means doing it analytically, coolly and without emotion.

clue.text: Hear a pal in rap, changing bits and pieces

indicators.note: the letters change places

explanation.surface: You listen to a friend performing in a rap, switching between different parts.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder reads as a sentence about music, which hides the fact that it is exactly thirteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Paraphernalia are miscellaneous belongings or bits of equipment.

clue.text: Naval officer adapted drama, initially recasting Ariel

indicators.note: adapted means the letters are reworked, as a play is adapted
initially takes the first letter of recasting

explanation.surface: A director adapts a play and starts by recasting Ariel, the spirit in The Tempest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recasting' looks like the anagram signal, but only its first letter, R, is used. DRAMA, R and ARIEL are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: A rear admiral is a senior naval rank, just below vice admiral.

clue.text: Woollen cloth Irish plunged in Kentucky lake

parts.note: Erse is the Irish Gaelic language

explanation.surface: A bolt of wool from Ireland has been thrown into a lake in Kentucky.
explanation.walkthrough: An obscure word, so trust the pieces: the Irish plunges into the state, not the lake.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist textile name: kerseymere is a fine twilled cloth, a variant of kersey, so woollen cloth is its category.

clue.text: Fellow hiding current shame

parts.note: Stan is a man's name, any fellow
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A man conceals something he is currently ashamed of.
explanation.walkthrough: Fellow suggests F or a college don, but here it is just a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A stain on one's name is a mark of shame.

clue.text: Like Tom, confused about measure of distance

indicators.note: the letters of Like Tom are muddled

explanation.surface: Like Tom, someone is puzzled about how far something is.
explanation.walkthrough: About looks like a container or reversal signal, but it is RE, tacked on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A kilometre is a thousand metres, a unit of distance.

clue.text: Aim of Bill's deed followed by chaps in hospital department

indicators.note: the deed and chaps pieces sit in the hospital department

parts.note: ENT is the ear, nose and throat department

indicators.note: followed by puts the chaps after the deed

explanation.surface: A man named Bill does a deed and is followed by chaps into a hospital department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a person; it is a parliamentary bill, a draft law.
explanation.definitionFit: A parliamentary bill aims to become law through enactment, its passing into statute.

clue.text: Former PM endlessly surrounded by regularly stark gossip

indicators.note: surrounded by means the shortened prime minister sits inside the other letters
regularly takes every other letter of stark
endlessly drops the last letter of the prime minister's name

parts.note: Clement Attlee was British Prime Minister 1945-51

explanation.surface: An ex-premier is endlessly hemmed in by blunt tittle-tattle.
explanation.walkthrough: Clement Attlee led Britain's post-war Labour government; the even letters of stark are the ones kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A tattler is a person who tattles, spreading chatter about others, so a gossip.

clue.text: Glorify Good Queen providing accommodation for fifty

parts.note: Good Queen Bess was Elizabeth I's nickname

explanation.surface: Praise be to the kindly queen who put up fifty guests.
explanation.walkthrough: Good looks like G, but 'Good Queen' together is Bess, the popular name for Elizabeth I.
explanation.definitionFit: A religious sense: to bless God, as in hymns and psalms, is to praise and extol Him.

clue.text: Club employee, a lively, energetic individual!

definitions.meaning: the doorman who keeps order at a nightclub

explanation.surface: A nightclub worker is praised as bubbly and full of beans.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is literal and jokey: anyone who bounces is a bouncer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bouncer is the heavy on a club's door, and also one who bounces.

clue.text: Dam river in Kent perhaps, the place of one's birth

parts.note: a dam is an animal's mother

indicators.note: the river is placed in the county, the way a river runs through one

parts.note: Kent is an English county; perhaps marks an example

explanation.surface: A dam holds back a river somewhere in Kent, where someone was born.
explanation.walkthrough: Dam wants to be a barrage across the river, but here it is a mother, as in horse breeding.
explanation.definitionFit: Your mother country is the land you were born in.

clue.text: Birds Greek character captured in French art

explanation.surface: Some birds and a Greek figure appear in a French painting.
explanation.walkthrough: Art is the old verb, as in 'thou art', not painting.
explanation.definitionFit: Emus are large flightless Australian birds.

clue.text: Increasingly accepting nearly everyone's state of mind

indicators.note: cuts the last letter from ALL

explanation.surface: Nearly everyone is growing more tolerant in their outlook.
explanation.walkthrough: Accepting reads as tolerant, an attitude that fits the state of mind, but it only means holding.
explanation.definitionFit: Morale is the confidence and spirit of a person or group.

clue.text: Obstruction demanded to protect part of canal

parts.note: a lock is a section of canal with gates

explanation.surface: Guards were ordered to defend a canal lock against a barricade.
explanation.walkthrough: Demanded is the old past tense bade, which few solvers reach for first.
explanation.definitionFit: A military sense: a blockade cuts off a port or city, an obstruction on a large scale.

clue.text: Some article — extremely newsy!

indicators.note: takes the letters at the extremes of newsy

parts.note: first and last letters of newsy

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece is packed with news.
explanation.walkthrough: Some leads the clue and looks like a hidden-word signal, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Have you any?' and 'have you some?' mean the same.

clue.text: Income, sad to say, taken back by railway

indicators.note: something taken back returns the way it came

explanation.surface: Sadly, someone's pay has been cut by the rail company.
explanation.walkthrough: Taken back reads as reclaimed money, but it only reverses ALAS.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym narrowed: a salary is the fixed income paid for a job, one kind of income.

clue.text: Poet's mature relationship with nature, for example

definitions.meaning: reads as a poet's grown-up bond, but mature is just a word the poet might use at a line's end
nature is the partner word: the endings are spelt alike but sound different

explanation.surface: A poet has grown into a grown-up bond with the natural world.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like Wordsworth's love of nature, but mature and nature are the pair: spelt alike at the end, pronounced differently.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye rhyme is a pair of words that match in spelling but not in sound.
